source_text: Cum autem noster numerus semper de deorum cultoribus augeatur, numquam uero, ne in ipsa quidem persecutione minuatur — quoniam peccare homines et inquinari sacrificio possunt, auerti autem non possunt a deo: ualet enim ui sua ueritas — quis est tandem tam excors tamque caecus quin uideat in utra sit parte sapientia? sed illi malitia et furore caecantur, ne uideant, stultosque esse arbitrantur qui cum habeant in potestate supplicia uitare, cruciari tamen et emori malunt, cum possint ex eo ipso peruidere non esse stultitiam in quam tanta hominum milia per orbem totum una et pari mente consentiant. si enim feminae sexus innrmitate labuntur - nam interdum isti muliebrem aut anilem superstitionem uocant — uiri certe sapiunt. si pueri, si adulescentes inprouidi sunt per aetatem, maturi certe ac senes habent stabile iudicium. si una ciuitas desipit, ceterae utique innumerabiles stultae esse non possunt. si una prouincia, una natio prudentia caret, ceteras omnes habere intellegentiam recti necesse est. cum uero ab ortu solis usque ad occasum lei diuina suscepta sit et omnis sexus, omnis aetas et gens et regio unis ac paribus animis deo seruiat, eadem sit ubique patientia, idem contemtus mortis, intellegere debuerant aliquid in ea re esse rationis quod non sine causa usque ad mortem defendatur, aliquid fundamenti ac soliditatis quod eam religionem non tantum iniuriis et uexatione non soluat, sed augeat semper et faciat firmiorem. nam et in hoc quoque illorum malitia conuincitur, quod euertisse se funditus religionem dei opinantur, si homines inquinauerint, cum et deo satisfacere liceat et nullus sit tam malus dei cultor quin data facultate ad placandum deum reuertatur et quidem deuotione maiore. peccati enim conscientia et metus poenae religiosiorem facit et semper multo firmior est fides quam reponit paenitentia. si ergo ipsi cum deos sibi arbitrantur iratos, tamen donis et sacrificiis et odoribus placari eos credunt, quid est tandem cur deum nostrum tam inmitem, tam inplacabilem putent, ut uideatur is iam Christianus esse non posse qui diis eorum coactus inuitusque libarit? nisi forte contaminatos semel putant animum translaturos, ut sua sponte iam facere incipiant quod per tormenta fecerunt. quis id officium libens obeat quod ab iniuria coepit? quis cum uideat laterum suorum cicatrices, non magis oderit deos, propter quos aeterna poenarum insignia et inpressas uisceribus suis notas gestet? ita fit ut data diuinitus pace et qui fugerunt uniuersi redeant et alius propter miraculum uirtutis nouus populus accedat. nam cum uideat uulgus dilacerari homines uariis tormentorum generibus et inter fatigatos carnifices inuictam tenere patientiam, existimant, id quod res est, nec consensum tam multorum nec perseuerantiam morientium uanam esse nec ipsam patientiam sine deo cruciatus tantos posse superare. latrones et robusti corporis uiri eiusmodi lacerationes perferre non queunt, exclamant et gemitus edunt, uincuntur enim dolore, quia deest illis inspirata patientia: nostri autem, ut de uiris taceam, pueri et mulierculae tortores suos taciti uincunt et exprimere illis gemitum nec ignis potest. eant Romani et Mucio glorientur aut Regulo, quorum alter necandum se hostibus tradidit, quod captiuum puduit uiuere, alter ab hostibus deprehensus cum uideret mortem se uitare non posse, manum foco iniecit, ut pro facinore suo satisfaceret hosti quem uoluit occidere, eaque poena ueniam quam non meruerat accepit: ecce sexus infirmus et fragilis aetas dilacerari se toto corpore urique perpetitur non necessitate, quia licet uitare si uelint, sed uoluntate, quia confidunt deo. haec est uera uirtus, quam philosophi quoque gloriabundi non re, sed uerbis inanibus iactant disserentes nihil esse tam congruens uiri sapientis grauitati atque constantiae quam nullis terroribus de sententia et proposito posse depelli, sed tanti esse cruciari et emori, ne fidem prodat, ne ab officio discedat, ne metu mortis aut dolore acerbo subactus aliquid faciat iniustum: nisi forte delirare illis uidetur Flaccus in lyricis, cum dicit: iustum et tenacem propositi uirum non ciuium ardor praua iubentium, uon uultus instantis tyranni mente quatit solida. quo nihil uerius dici potest, si hoc ad eos referatur qui nullos, cruciatus, nullam mortem recusant, ne a fide iustitiaque declinent, qui non tyrannicas iussiones, non praesidum gladios tremunt, quominus ueram et solidam libertatem constanti mente defendant, quae in hoc solo tuenda sapienti est. quis enim tam insolens, tam elatus est qui me uetet oculos in caelum tollere, qui inponat mihi necessitatem uel colendi quod nolim uel quod uelim non colendi? quid iam nobis ulterius relinquatur, si etiam hoc quod uoluntate fieri oportet libido extorqueat aliena? nemo istut efficiet, si quid nobis ad contemnendam mortem doloremque uirtutis est. quam constantiam si tenemus, cur stulti iudicamur facientes ea quae philosophi laudant? recte igitur Seneca incongruentiam hominibus obiectans ait: summa uirtus illis uidetur magnus animus, et idem eum qui contemnit mortem pro furioso habent: quod est utique summae peruersitatis. sed hi uanarum religionum cultores eadem stultitia id obiciunt qua uerum deum non intellegunt: quos Sibylla Erythraea xuxpoy ? et avoTQVOj ; uocat, surdos scilicet et excordes, qui nec audiant diuina nec sentiant, sed terram digitis suis imaginatam metuant et adorent.
pass_a_gloss: Our number always grows from the worshipers of the gods and is never lessened even in persecution, since humans can sin and be defiled by sacrifice but cannot be turned away from God: for truth is strong by its own force. They think they have overturned God's religion if they have defiled people, yet one may make satisfaction to God, and conscience of sin with fear of punishment makes one more religious, and the faith that penitence restores is always much firmer. This is true virtue: to be tortured and to die rather than betray faith or leave duty; true and solid freedom is to defend with constant mind the right to worship what one wills and not to worship what one does not will.
pass_b_english: But since our number is always increased from the worshipers of the gods, and is never lessened even in the persecution itself — because humans can sin and be defiled by sacrifice, but cannot be turned away from God: for truth is strong by its own force — who at last is so senseless and so blind that he does not see on which side wisdom is? But they are blinded by malice and fury, that they may not see, and they think those foolish who, though they have it in their power to avoid punishments, prefer nonetheless to be tortured and to die, though from this very fact they could perceive that that is not folly into which so many thousands of humans throughout the whole world agree with one and the same mind. If women slip by the weakness of their sex — for sometimes they call this a womanish or old-womanish superstition — men at least are wise. If boys and youths are improvident by age, the mature and the old at least have stable judgment. If one city is mad, the rest beyond number cannot be foolish. If one province or one nation lacks prudence, all the others must have understanding of what is right. But when from the rising of the sun even to its setting the divine law has been taken up, and every sex, every age and people and region serves God with one and equal minds, and there is the same patience everywhere, the same contempt of death, they ought to have understood that there is something of reason in that matter which is defended not without cause even unto death, something of foundation and solidity which not only does not dissolve that religion by injuries and vexation, but always increases it and makes it firmer.

For in this too their malice is convicted: that they think they have overturned God's religion from the foundation if they have defiled humans, though both it is allowed to make satisfaction to God, and there is no worshiper of God so bad that, when opportunity is given, he does not return to appeasing God, and indeed with greater devotion. For conscience of sin and fear of punishment makes one more religious, and the faith that penitence puts back is always much firmer. If therefore they themselves, when they think the gods angry at them, still believe them to be appeased by gifts and sacrifices and incense, why at last do they think our God so harsh, so implacable, that he who has poured a libation to their gods under compulsion and unwillingly should seem already unable to be a Christian? Unless perhaps they think that those once contaminated will transfer their mind so that they begin of their own will to do what they did through torments. Who would willingly take up that service which began from injury? Who, when he sees the scars of his sides, would not rather hate the gods for whose sake he bears everlasting marks of punishments and brands pressed into his flesh? So it happens that when peace is given from heaven, both all who fled return and another new people is added because of the miracle of virtue. For when the crowd sees humans torn by various kinds of torments and, among worn-out executioners, holding an unconquered patience, they judge — which is the fact — that neither the consent of so many nor the perseverance of those dying is empty, nor that patience itself can overcome such great tortures without God. Robbers and men of strong body cannot endure lacerations of that kind: they cry out and give groans, for they are conquered by pain, because inspired patience is absent from them. But ours — to say nothing of men — boys and weak women silently conquer their torturers, and not even fire can wring a groan from them.

This is true virtue, which the philosophers too, glorying, toss about not in deed but in empty words, discoursing that nothing so befits the gravity and constancy of a wise man as that he cannot be driven by any terrors from his opinion and purpose, but that it is worth so much to be tortured and to die, lest he betray faith, lest he depart from duty, lest, subdued by fear of death or bitter pain, he do anything unjust — unless perhaps Flaccus seems to them to rave in his lyrics when he says that the just man, tenacious of purpose, is not shaken in solid mind by the citizens' heat ordering what is crooked, nor by the face of the pressing tyrant. Nothing truer can be said, if this is referred to those who refuse no tortures, no death, lest they decline from faith and justice, who do not tremble at tyrannical orders or the swords of governors so as not to defend with constant mind true and solid freedom, which in this alone is to be guarded by the wise. For who is so insolent, so lifted up, that he forbids me to lift my eyes to heaven, that he lays on me the necessity either of worshiping what I do not will or of not worshiping what I will? What further is left to us, if even this which ought to be done by will alien lust wrings out? No one will accomplish that, if we have any virtue for despising death and pain. If we hold that constancy, why are we judged fools for doing the things the philosophers praise? Rightly therefore Seneca, objecting incongruity to humans, says: the highest virtue seems to them a great mind, and yet the same people hold him who despises death for a madman — which is certainly of the highest perversity. But these worshipers of empty religions object that by the same folly by which they do not understand the true God: whom the Erythraean Sibyl calls deaf and senseless, who neither hear divine things nor perceive them, but fear and adore earth imagined by their own fingers.

lemmas.form: ne fidem prodat…ueram et solidam libertatem
lemmas.gloss: die rather than betray faith; defend free worship

choices.why: Sacrifice can defile, but truth's force keeps them from being turned from God.

rejected: one libation under torture forever bars return
choices.why: Penitence restores a firmer faith; the coerced often hate the gods more.

rejected: philosophers alone own contempt of death
choices.why: True virtue: suffer rather than betray faith; freedom is to worship by will.
